A country spending 40% of its national budget (i.e. tax money) on welfare is by itself not a bad thing at all. This is just putting the public social spending into context with other public spending, for instance on the military and on public infrastructure. In isolation, it says precious little about how much of our productivity goes into social spending.

An arguably much better measure for "how much of country's resources go into welfare" is to look at social expenditure (which includes welfare) as a percentage of the gross domestic product, not as a percentage of the public household. Variables such as "how big is your army", "how much do you spend for roads", and "how high are your taxes anyway" all play no role when you look at that number. So this is the number that is commonly used to compare social expenditure between countries.

I won't go into detail, but here's one OECD report that compares social expenditure between all its member states. Just glance over it and you'll get a good feel for how Norway compares to its peers. "Ctrl+f norway" will also lead to some interesting bits. You'll see that Norway is somewhere in the middle of the big group of countries that spend comparably much on welfare, so in no way is it "the one country in the world that uses most money per capita on welfare-benefits" like you wrote.

I guess you could say this ("most money per capita on welfare") only if you converted all the currencies into dollars, and if you in addition completely ignore the cost-of-living which also vary vastly among the countries being compared.
